article.overview: A lunar hopping robot is a small surface mobility payload that moves by jumping rather than by continuous rolling or walking. Hopping can carry a robot over boulders, out of a landing area and into terrain such as crater floors and permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) that are difficult for conventional rovers. One lunar hopper has a documented surface activity: JAXA's LEV-1 executed planned leaping movements on the Moon in January 2024 [1]. China's Chang'e-7 mission plans a mobile hopper for shadowed craters, but it had not launched when the sources reviewed were published [2]. Intuitive Machines' Micro-Nova "Grace" hopper was funded under a NASA award and was planned for lunar delivery [3][4], but no source reviewed confirms that it deployed or hopped. The class therefore has one confirmed lunar surface demonstration, several planned or unverified lunar hoppers, and several ground or asteroid demonstrations.
article.description: A lunar hopping robot typically has a body that holds its sensing, computing, power and communications equipment, plus a propulsion or energy-storage mechanism that launches it into a ballistic flight. Between hops, the robot lands, may reorient itself, and then repeats the cycle. Depending on the design, the hop may be produced by rocket-type propulsion [3], by an internal motor that drives a rebound [5][6], or by springs that store energy at landing and release it at take-off [8]. Some concepts combine hopping with wheels or legs for ground driving. The NASA NIAC Spelunker concept, for example, envisaged multiple hybrid driving/hopping robots exploring caves [7]. Hopping is not a single standardised design, and the examples in this article differ widely in mass, size, sensing and maturity.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Hoppers are intended to extend a robot's reach into places that are hard to access by wheels. For PSRs, which may hold water ice and other volatiles, the Chang'e-7 hopper is described as carrying a water-molecule analyzer and as designed for multiple flights into dark, cold, shadowed craters [2]. Intuitive Machines' Micro-Nova concept aimed to take the first images from inside a PSR, with black-and-white coverage of about half of the PSR and temperature measurements estimated at 40 to 80 kelvin [4]. The same concept included high-resolution stereo imaging of sunlit areas [4]. For caves and skylights, NASA NIAC's Spelunker concept proposed a tethered power and communications hub at a skylight rim, with hopping robots exploring the void below [7]. JAXA described LEV-1's leaping movements and inter-robot radio test as demonstrations of its capabilities [1].
article.operating_principle:
Gravity is the central constraint. Lunar surface gravity is roughly one-sixth of Earth's. For a given take-off speed, a hop reaches about six times the height and range, and lasts about six times as long, as the same hop on Earth. The hop itself is generated by releasing stored or applied energy that gives the body a take-off velocity. Several mechanisms are documented:

- Rocket-type propulsion, as described for Micro-Nova [3].
- An internal motor that drives a rebound, as described for the MINERVA-II1 rovers on asteroid Ryugu [5][6].
- Leg springs that store energy during landing and release it at take-off, with a reaction wheel for in-flight orientation, as described for the SpaceBok quadruped [8].

The mechanism used by LEV-1 is not described in the JAXA release reviewed [1].

After each landing, the robot must determine its orientation and position before the next hop. The SpaceBok team reported that higher jumps make stabilisation during flight and a safe landing more difficult [8].
article.scientific_importance: Hoppers matter because lunar terrain of high scientific interest may be inaccessible or dangerous to wheeled rovers, and because shadowed regions may hold volatile resources that can be characterised only by in-situ measurement. Hopping has already been demonstrated on a small body: the JAXA MINERVA-II1 Rover-1B hop was confirmed on 23 September 2018 on asteroid Ryugu [6]. JAXA's LEV-1 leaping on the Moon is a documented lunar demonstration [1]. However, the scientific value of any single hopper depends on sensor quality, operating life and communications, and these remain unverified for most designs in this article.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar hopping robot. The example designs below range from a lunar surface system to concepts and asteroid rovers, so their numbers should not be compared as if they described the same class of hardware. Values not stated in the cited sources are described as not publicly specified.

examples.name: JAXA SLIM LEV-1
examples.type: Flown lunar surface hopping rover (lunar surface, January 2024)
examples.status: Flown; operated on the lunar surface
examples.mass_note: 2.1 kg including a 90 g communication device, per the JAXA release. Some press coverage gives 2.3 kg; the discrepancy is not resolved.
examples.dimensions: Not stated in the JAXA release reviewed.
examples.leaping_mechanism: Not described in the JAXA release reviewed.
examples.hop_count: Not stated in the JAXA release reviewed.
examples.communications: Telemetry sent directly to ground stations; JAXA describes the direct link as covering approximately 380,000 km.
examples.outcome: Image acquisition on the lunar surface had not been confirmed at the time of the release. After the designated power was depleted, LEV-1 entered standby; JAXA said it would keep trying to receive its signals.
examples.notes: No image assets verified in this draft.

examples.name: Intuitive Machines Micro-Nova "Grace"
examples.type: Lunar hopper lander (in development as of 2021; flight status unconfirmed)
examples.status: In development as of July 2021 reporting. Delivery planned on a Nova-C lander for December 2022; IM-2 landed on its side in March 2025. No source reviewed confirms that the hopper deployed or hopped.
examples.mass_note: Total mass not stated in the cited article.
examples.dimensions: With landing gear, 76.2 cm in length, width and height.
examples.payload_capability: Carries a 1 kg payload more than 2.5 km.
examples.funding: $41.6 million NASA Tipping Point award, announced 16 July 2021.
examples.science_partner: Arizona State University (School of Earth and Space Exploration).
examples.planned_measurements: High-resolution colour images near the hopper; black-and-white images covering about half of a permanently shadowed region; high-resolution stereo images in sunlit areas; temperature estimated at 40 to 80 K inside the PSR.
examples.notes: Spaceflight Now mentions the Grace hopper only in a funding context. IM-2 landed about 250 m from its intended site inside a crater, on its side; the company said it did not expect the lander to recharge and that the mission had concluded.

examples.name: Chang'e-7 mobile hopper
examples.status: Planned for launch in the second half of 2026 on a Long March 5 from Wenchang; press reports conflict on the date, including one that suggests 2027.
examples.mass_note: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.description: Described as a hopper, sometimes described as a mini-flying probe with legs, that carries a water-molecule analyzer; designed for multiple flights and for landings in dark, cold, shadowed craters.
examples.propulsion_and_hop_range: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.notes: The hopper is one of four spacecraft in the mission (orbiter, lander, rover and hopper). Deployment method is not publicly specified.

examples.name: JAXA MINERVA-II1 Rover-1A and Rover-1B
examples.type: Flown hopping rovers on asteroid Ryugu (2018); not a lunar payload
examples.status: Flown; Rover-1B hop confirmed on 23 September 2018 (JST).
examples.hop_mechanism: An internal motor rotates and causes the rover to hop during the rebound.
examples.expected_performance: Before deployment, JAXA expected each hop to keep the rover airborne for up to 15 minutes and to travel up to 15 m horizontally.
examples.confirmed_performance: Hop height, duration and distance not stated in the release reviewed.
examples.notes: Included as a well-documented flown hopping mechanism, not as lunar hardware.

examples.name: SpaceBok
examples.status: Ground-tested at ESA ESTEC in controlled facilities; not flown. Article labelled as archive content dated 4 July 2019.
examples.jump_performance: Jumps of up to 1.3 m in simulated lunar gravity. Projected lunar jump of up to 2 m, which is an estimate and not a demonstrated result.
examples.control: In-flight orientation controlled with a reaction wheel; springs in the legs store energy at landing and release it at take-off.
examples.notes: No image assets verified in this draft.

examples.name: LunaRoo
examples.type: Hopping lunar science platform (prototype stage at most)
examples.status: Prototype milestones listed (2016); the page does not state whether any prototype was tested in simulation or flown.
examples.dimensions: Designed to be compact enough to fit within a 10 cm cube.
examples.hop_target: Target hop of up to 20 m above the surface. No measured hop performance is reported.
examples.environmental_requirement: Electronics to withstand -153 to 123 degrees C.
examples.notes: The original QUT page URL carried a query parameter (p=2849), which was removed under the URL policy. The cleaned address may not resolve to the same page and must be checked before publication.

examples.name: NASA NIAC Spelunker
examples.status: Concept study; no flight hardware indicated in the page reviewed.
examples.configuration: Multiple hybrid driving/hopping robots and a tethered power and communications hub for exploring skylights and caves. Partners: Astrobotic Technology and Carnegie Mellon University; William Whittaker led the project.
examples.technology_maturity: Robot configuration, subsurface terrain modelling and in-cave autonomy advanced to TRL 3. The starting TRL is not stated.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The examples cannot be ranked on a single scale. LEV-1's dimensions are not stated in the release reviewed. The MINERVA-II1 rovers are hexagonal with a diameter of 18 cm and a height of 7 cm. Micro-Nova's 76.2 cm overall size with landing gear refers to a hopper that carries a 1 kg payload, not to a compact hopping body. LunaRoo's 10 cm figure is a design target. SpaceBok's dimensions are not given. The Chang'e-7 hopper's dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The stated masses are 2.1 kg for LEV-1 (including a 90 g communication device) and about 1.1 kg each for the MINERVA-II1 rovers. Micro-Nova's total mass is not stated. The Chang'e-7 hopper's mass is not publicly specified. Mass values should be read with the design context: a surface hopper that carries a communications device, a lunar-gravity hop, and an asteroid rover with a motor-driven rebound are not the same class of hardware.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No power figure is stated for any example in the sources reviewed. LEV-1 is recorded as having depleted its designated power and entered standby. Power design for a lunar hopper operating in a PSR is not given in any source reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Hopping robots face the lunar environment's vacuum, thermal extremes, dust and surface-impact loads. Thermal design is a central constraint. LunaRoo's electronics requirement of -153 to 123 degrees C is one stated design range [9]. Micro-Nova's planned PSR temperature measurement was estimated at 40 to 80 K [4]. This indicates the thermal environment that the instrument would need to measure, not only survive.

Hops add dynamic requirements, including in-flight attitude control and stabilised landings. The SpaceBok team identified these as harder at higher jumps [8]. Communications must support the robot through the hop cycle. LEV-1 maintained a direct link to ground stations [1]. Operation in PSRs requires the robot to function without direct sunlight, so the power source and battery design are central. No source reviewed gives a power design for a lunar hopper in a PSR.
article.limitations: Hopping introduces risks that wheeled rovers do not have. These include poorly controlled landings, loss of orientation, damage on landing and dependence on accurate hop planning. Hop range and height depend on take-off speed, which depends on the propulsion or energy-storage design, so no general figure applies. A successful hop does not guarantee a complete science return: LEV-1 hopped but did not confirm image acquisition [1]. Lander orientation can also block other payloads on the same mission. On IM-2, the lander's attitude prevented the TRIDENT drill from penetrating the surface and prevented deployment of the MAPP rover [3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: This is a surface payload. Typical stages are integration with a lander or mission stack on Earth, launch, lunar transfer, landing, deployment, setup of power, data and thermal interfaces, and then hopping.
transportation_process: Integrate the hopper with a lander or mission stack on Earth.
Transfer to the Moon and land on the surface.
Deploy the hopper from the lander, or stow and release it according to the design.
Set up power, data and thermal interfaces, then begin hop operations.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: LEV-1 was released from the SLIM lander and then executed leaping movements [1]. The MINERVA-II1 rovers were stored in a container and deployed on Ryugu before hopping [5]. Micro-Nova was planned in 2021 to be delivered by a Nova-C lander [4]. Chang'e-7's hopper deployment method and interfaces are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed [2].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The LEV-1 release from SLIM and the MINERVA-II1 container deployment are the best-documented deployment examples in this article [1][5]. The IM-2 landing orientation affected other payloads on the same mission [3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility claim is made for any named lander, rover or spacecraft. The 2021 plan named a Nova-C lander for Micro-Nova delivery [4], but no interface evidence was reviewed that would confirm compatibility. Mass, dimensions, mounting, landing-load, power and data interface data needed for such an assessment are not public for most examples.

article.historical_significance: JAXA describes LEV-1 and LEV-2 as Japan's first lunar exploration robots, and it reports leaping movements and direct communication with Earth for LEV-1 [1]. The MINERVA-II1 Rover-1B hop on Ryugu in 2018 demonstrated hopping mobility on a small body [6]. The Micro-Nova and Chang'e-7 hopper programmes show that dedicated hopper payloads are now in development or planned for polar shadowed craters [2][4]. Spelunker and LunaRoo are concepts or prototypes. Their significance is conceptual, not operational [7][9].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The following items remain unverified. LEV-1's hop count and mechanism are not stated in the primary JAXA release reviewed [1]. Its mass conflicts across sources (2.1 kg in the JAXA release, 2.3 kg in press coverage) [1]. Image acquisition was not confirmed [1]. Micro-Nova's deployment and hop status are not confirmed by any source reviewed. The IM-2 report is from March 2025, and no later report was reviewed [3]. The development status described in 2021 may be outdated [4]. Chang'e-7 hopper mass, dimensions, propulsion, hop range and deployment method are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed, and launch timing conflicts across reports [2]. SpaceBok and LunaRoo data come from a 2019 archive article and an undated project page [8][9]. Spelunker's starting TRL is not stated [7]. Operating durations for the MINERVA-II1 rovers reported in secondary search results were not verified and are omitted. No direct image assets were verified for this draft, so no images are included. The QUT source URL carried a query parameter, which was removed; the cleaned address may not resolve to the same page and should be checked before publication [9].

No direct image asset URLs were verified from official pages in this run, so no images were included. Image research is outstanding.
LEV-1 mass conflicts across sources: 2.1 kg (including a 90 g communication device) per the JAXA release used as primary; 2.3 kg in secondary press coverage. Unresolved.
Micro-Nova deployment and hop status are not confirmed by any source reviewed. The 2021 development status and December 2022 delivery plan are outdated.

Chang'e-7 launch date conflicts across press reports (second half of 2026 per the Planetary Society; one report suggests 2027). Hopper mass, dimensions, propulsion and deployment method are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

Operating durations for the MINERVA-II1 rovers and a reported count of six LEV-1 hops appeared only in secondary search results and were not verified; they are omitted from the article and JSON.
The Spelunker NIAC page does not state the starting TRL; the reported TRL 3 is the end-of-study level for three technologies.
